summary:
Whattarpu is a light mobile web app that helps family farmers in Puno, Peru, decide what to sow and when as frost and dry years become harder to predict. In 2025, Puno's farm output fell 9.6%, and frost hit about 70% of its potato area in January.

The farmer pins their plot on a map and answers six simple questions. Whattarpu combines more than 40 years of NASA POWER daily climate (since 1981), NASA satellite imagery and SRTM elevation with Peru's official crop guides (INIA) and FAO ECOCROP requirements. It returns three crop rotations: their usual one and two alternatives, each showing how well the crop withstands frost and drought, the best sowing date and the source of every rule. A 7-day frost alert compares the coming nights with the cold that damages their crop.

It uses explicit rules, not AI, so the same answers always give the same result. It works on low-end phones, in simple Spanish, with read-aloud, and keeps working offline after the first visit. It matters because it turns NASA data into one decision a farmer makes every season.
details:
What it does. Whattarpu answers one question a farmer faces every season: what should I sow on this plot, and when? The first version covers Puno, Peru's department with the most registered producers (207,598) and the department with the most population, districts and farmland at high drought risk for El Niño 2026–2027. Most farmers there are family producers who mix crops and livestock, and 40% of highland producers are 60 or older.

How it works.

1. Locate the plot. Province, district and village (110 districts and 9,372 villages from Peru's INEI), GPS, or a pin on a NASA satellite or street map. The app reads the elevation of that exact point.

2. Read the zone's climate. From NASA POWER daily minimum temperature and rainfall since 1981: frost nights per month, nights below each crop's damaging temperature, and dry years using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI, WMO method). Soil pH and texture come from SoilGrids, or from the farmer's own soil test.

3. Ask six questions. Previous crop, years since the last fallow, irrigation, how the land is worked, the farmer's priority (food, fodder or sale) and the sowing month.

4. Apply explicit rules. A catalog of 14 crops grown in Puno, with sowing windows from INIA and requirements (temperature, rainfall, pH, texture, elevation, killing frost) from INIA or, when no local value exists, FAO ECOCROP. Rotation rules come from INIA, such as avoiding potato after potato because of the cyst nematode, and the traditional aynoka sequence.

5. Show three rotations. The usual one and two alternatives, each with sowing date, calendar, frost and drought tolerance, why, evidence, benefits, unknowns and risks, all linked to sources.

6. During the season. Crop progress, the month's historical frost risk, vegetation vigor from MODIS NDVI, and a 7-day frost alert for the plot compared with the crop's damaging temperature. It is labeled as a forecast, not an official warning, and links to Senamhi's official warnings.

Benefits. It turns 45 years of satellite-based climate into a choice a farmer can act on, at plot level. It compares crops by how much frost and drought they withstand, since the climate of the zone is the same for every option. Every rule shows its source, so technicians and farmers can check it.

Design for the user. Large buttons and icons, simple Spanish, read-aloud, one question per screen, works on low-end phones and offline after the first visit. The app stores no personal data.

What we hope to achieve. Field tests with farmers in Puno through our agronomist, adding sowing dates from the start of the rainy season (NASA POWER) for more crops, a sourced table of actions against frost, and then other Andean regions by adding data only.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules (no build step, no framework), Leaflet maps, a service worker for offline use, the browser's Web Speech API, Node.js scripts and GitHub Actions to download NASA POWER data, automated tests (node:test and Playwright), ESLint, and hosting on GitHub Pages.

Team. Samantha Milla (Product Lead & Developer), Gabriela Ayala (Agronomy Lead), Elena Silva (Livestock & User Advisor).

Code: https://github.com/samsfall/whattarpu

Executive presentation and project documents: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a0LATboFKpylZjXNwjuAYgbYKfD9NDFX?usp=sharing
